claim: A CD73 blockade was shown to result in tumor inhibition from recruitment of NK cells.
source: Prior evidence also supports this approach, as a CD73 blockade Antonioli et al., 2016; Geoghegan et al., 2016 was shown to result in tumor inhibition from recruitment of NK cells Wang et al., 2018, and an increase in the presence of IFN-γ and perforin Young et al., 2016; Häusler et al., 2014.
evidence: Supported by citations to Antonioli et al., 2016; Geoghegan et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018

claim: A CD73 blockade was shown to result in an increase in the presence of IFN-γ and perforin.
source: Prior evidence also supports this approach, as a CD73 blockade Antonioli et al., 2016; Geoghegan et al., 2016 was shown to result in tumor inhibition from recruitment of NK cells Wang et al., 2018, and an increase in the presence of IFN-γ and perforin Young et al., 2016; Häusler et al., 2014.
evidence: Supported by citations to Young et al., 2016; Häusler et al., 2014

claim: Under hypoxia, cancer cells express HIF-1α, which helps to increase adenosine accumulation.
source: Under hypoxia, cancer cells express HIF-1α, which helps to increase adenosine accumulation, but NK cells have impaired killing ability and lowered expression of NKG2D and intracellular perforin and granzyme B (Solocinski et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Solocinski et al., 2020

claim: Under hypoxia, NK cells have impaired killing ability and lowered expression of NKG2D and intracellular perforin and granzyme B.
source: Under hypoxia, cancer cells express HIF-1α, which helps to increase adenosine accumulation, but NK cells have impaired killing ability and lowered expression of NKG2D and intracellular perforin and granzyme B (Solocinski et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Solocinski et al., 2020

claim: CD73.CAR NK cells were able to rescue the detrimental effects of hypoxia to increase NK cell killing ability through the blocking of adenosine.
source: We also show decreased NK killing under hypoxic conditions; however, the CD73.CAR NK cells were able to rescue the detrimental effects of hypoxia to increase NK cell killing ability through the blocking of adenosine.
evidence: Supported by hypoxia killing data

claim: NK cells express HIF-1α under hypoxic conditions that cause downregulation of killing ability.
source: NK cells also express HIF-1α under hypoxic conditions that cause this downregulation of killing ability.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about NK cell response to hypoxia

claim: Targeting HIF-1α directly in the NK cell could potentially be disadvantageous by impairing tumor killing and NK infiltration.
source: HIF-1α has been under investigation as an anti-tumor strategy but targeting HIF-1α directly in the NK cell could potentially be disadvantageous by impairing tumor killing and NK infiltration Krzywinska et al., 2017.
evidence: Supported by citation to Krzywinska et al., 2017

claim: By targeting adenosine accumulation directly, the effects of hypoxia on the cancer cells will be diminished, while not affecting the killing ability of the NK cells.
source: Therefore, by targeting adenosine accumulation directly, the effects of hypoxia on the cancer cells will be diminished, while not affecting the killing ability of the NK cells.
evidence: Inferred from the mechanism of CD73 targeting

claim: CD73 expression on non-tumor locations normally supports a variety of physiological processes to prevent an overactive immune system.
source: CD73 expression on non-tumor locations normally supports a variety of physiological processes to prevent an overactive immune system, and these locations include some epithelial cells, endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and cardiac myocytes Kordaß et al., 2018.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kordaß et al., 2018

claim: No broad adverse safety effects have been reported in clinical studies targeting CD73 with systemically administered antibodies.
source: Although no broad adverse safety effects have been reported in clinical studies targeting CD73 with systemically administered antibodies Harvey et al., 2020; Siu et al., 2018, a strategy to reduce the risk of targeting non-tumor tissue has been to engineer the antibodies without Fc receptor engagement.
evidence: Supported by citations to Harvey et al., 2020; Siu et al., 2018

claim: Recent data from the MEDI9447 trial reported that systemic anti-CD73 therapy was well-tolerated with a manageable safety profile.
source: Recent data from the MEDI9447 trial reported that systemic anti-CD73 therapy was well-tolerated with a manageable safety profile Geoghegan et al., 2016; Overman et al., 2018.
evidence: Supported by citations to Geoghegan et al., 2016; Overman et al., 2018

claim: Eliminating the Fc engagement eliminates the induction of ADCC, thus restricting NK cell activation and efficacy of treatment.
source: However, eliminating the Fc engagement also eliminates the induction of ADCC, thus restricting NK cell activation and efficacy of treatment.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about ADCC mechanism

claim: NK cells did not have any observable off-target effects, as exhibited through killing experiments on endothelial cells.
source: Here we showed that inherently the NK cells did not have any observable off-target effects, as exhibited through killing experiments on endothelial cells.
evidence: Supported by HUVEC killing data

claim: Even with high CD73, NK cells do not target normal healthy tissues, thus able to avoid off-target activation against non-malignant cells.
source: Moreover, the engineered NK cells did not have an increase in killing, indicating that even with high CD73, NK cells do not target normal healthy tissues, thus able to avoid off-target activation against non-malignant cells.
evidence: Inferred from HUVEC killing data

claim: Concerns over the targeting of CD73-directed NK cells to non-tumor tissues can be alleviated by administering these cells locally, such as intratumorally.
source: While the use of HUVEC cells may have some limitations compared to normal endothelial cells, concerns over the targeting of CD73-directed NK cells to non-tumor tissues can be alleviated by administering these cells locally, such as intratumorally Dubinett et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2017.
evidence: Supported by citations to Dubinett et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2017

claim: The engineered NK cells with the anti-CD73 construct stunted tumor growth and promoted increased NK cell filtration into lung tumors in vivo.
source: Here, we also show that the engineered NK cells with the anti-CD73 construct stunted tumor growth and promoted increased NK cell filtration into lung tumors in vivo.
evidence: Supported by in vivo tumor growth and infiltration data

claim: CD73, as a tumor-associated antigen, is a viable target and mediates potent CAR-NK cell based anti-tumor effects against CD73+ lung adenocarcinoma xenografts in mice, both in terms of tumor metabolism and mouse survival.
source: These data point to CD73, as a tumor-associated antigen, being a viable target and mediating potent CAR-NK cell based anti-tumor effects against CD73+ lung adenocarcinoma xenografts in mice, both in terms of tumor metabolism and mouse survival.
evidence: Supported by in vivo tumor growth and survival data

claim: Clinical data has shown that adoptive transfer of cytokine-induced killer cells is well tolerated and provides improved outcomes over chemotherapy in treating NSCLC patients.
source: Clinical data has shown that adoptive transfer of cytokine-induced killer cells is well tolerated and provides improved outcomes over chemotherapy in treating NSCLC patients Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2014.
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2014

claim: NK cells can have a short lifespan, but the addition of multiple injections and IL-15 helps to drive NK expansion and persistence.
source: NK cells can have a short lifespan, but the addition of multiple injections and IL-15 helps to drive NK expansion and persistence Liu et al., 2018; Sahm et al., 2012; Hoyos et al., 2010.
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2018; Sahm et al., 2012; Hoyos et al., 2010

claim: Three doses of the engineered NK cells showed suppressed tumor growth after these three infusions.
source: In our study, we employed three doses of the engineered NK cells and showed suppressed tumor growth after these three infusions.
evidence: Supported by in vivo tumor growth data

claim: There was no evidence of toxicity of the CD73.CAR-NK treatment or with IL-15 as mice weights were consistent between treatment groups throughout the study.
source: We did not have any evidence of toxicity of our treatment or with IL-15 as mice weights were consistent between treatment groups throughout the study.
evidence: Supported by body weight data

claim: The NK cells were able to persist and maintain their cytotoxic potential as evidenced by the smaller tumor size and stunted tumor growth over time after treatment ended.
source: As evidenced by the smaller tumor size and stunted tumor growth over time after treatment ended, the NK cells were able to persist and maintain their cytotoxic potential.
evidence: Inferred from tumor growth data after treatment cessation

claim: At the end of treatment, NK cells were still found in the circulation.
source: At the end of treatment, NK cells were still found in the circulation, and the engineered CD73.CAR-NK cells were found to have infiltrated into the tumors more than the non-engineered NK cells.
evidence: Supported by NK cell detection data

claim: The engineered CD73.CAR-NK cells were found to have infiltrated into the tumors more than the non-engineered NK cells.
source: At the end of treatment, NK cells were still found in the circulation, and the engineered CD73.CAR-NK cells were found to have infiltrated into the tumors more than the non-engineered NK cells.
evidence: Supported by IHC infiltration data

claim: The granzyme B expression in the tumor microenvironment was much higher for the engineered NK cells.
source: There were no differences between activation and inhibitory receptors in circulating NK cells for engineered and non-engineered groups; however, the granzyme B expression in the TME was much higher for the engineered NK cells.
evidence: Supported by IHC granzyme B data

claim: Not all the cells in the circulation may have made it to the tumor site since the treatment was injected via the tail vein.
source: Since the treatment was injected via the tail vein, not all the cells in the circulation may have made it to the tumor site Ma et al., 2019; Wang and Matosevic, 2020.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma et al., 2019; Wang and Matosevic, 2020

claim: The increase in granzyme B in the tumor microenvironment for the engineered cells showed that the NK cells maintained their cytotoxic potential over the course of the study.
source: Moreover, the increase in granzyme B in the TME for the engineered cells showed that the NK cells maintained their cytotoxic potential over the course of the study.
evidence: Inferred from granzyme B expression data

claim: We cannot rule out whether the cytotoxic effect is dependent upon activation signaling through the CD16 domains or resulting from improved target cell conjugation to enhance natural cytotoxicity.
source: Although engagement of CD73.CAR with CD73 on the tumor cells promoted NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity, we have not directly tested the activation signaling function of our CD73.CAR construct. Therefore, we cannot rule out whether this effect is dependent upon activation signaling through the CD16 domains or resulting from improved target cell conjugation to enhance natural cytotoxicity.
evidence: Stated as limitation of the study

claim: NK cells have an advantage over the FDA approved T-cell therapies, as NK cells exert an innate killing ability that is non-CAR specific.
source: Therapeutically, NK cells have an advantage over the FDA approved T-cell therapies, as NK cells exert an innate killing ability that is non-CAR specific, as shown by the killing of tumor targets by non-engineered NK cells.
evidence: Supported by killing data from non-engineered NK cells

claim: Directing NK cells against CD73 in the tumor microenvironment can potentially eliminate CD73 expressing suppressor cells, such as CD73+ Tregs.
source: Directing NK cells against CD73 in the TME can also potentially eliminate CD73 expressing suppressor cells, such as CD73+ Tregs Chambers and Matosevic, 2019; Schuler et al., 2014.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chambers and Matosevic, 2019; Schuler et al., 2014

claim: Expression of CD73 on tumor-infiltrating NK cells is low.
source: Expression of CD73 on tumor-infiltrating NK cells is low (Chambers et al., 2022), as we and others have shown, but CD73+ NK cells were associated with a hyper-functional phenotype, including the ability to produce IL-10 (Neo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chambers et al., 2022

claim: CD73+ NK cells were associated with a hyper-functional phenotype, including the ability to produce IL-10.
source: Expression of CD73 on tumor-infiltrating NK cells is low (Chambers et al., 2022), as we and others have shown, but CD73+ NK cells were associated with a hyper-functional phenotype, including the ability to produce IL-10 (Neo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neo et al., 2020

claim: Targeting CD73 expressing cells in the tumor microenvironment will not only eliminate tumor-positive cells, but may remove additional cell populations that help support the tumor niche.
source: Therefore, targeting CD73 expressing cells in the TME will not only eliminate tumor-positive cells, but may remove these additional cell populations that help support the tumor niche.
evidence: Inferred from the role of CD73+ cells in the tumor microenvironment
